title: Minimum Jumps to Reach Home
constraints: The values in forbidden are distinct
signature: int minimumJumps(int[] forbidden, int a, int b, int x)
notes:
## Intuition

Every jump costs the same, so "fewest jumps" is a shortest path in an unweighted graph, which breadth-first search solves level by level. The catch is the "no two left jumps in a row" rule: whether the bug may jump left depends on how it arrived. So a node is the pair (position, did the last jump go left), and the same position can be visited twice, once in each state.

The line is infinite to the right, so the search needs a right edge. A known bound says an optimal route never has to pass `max(x, max(forbidden)) + a + b`: beyond the last forbidden spot and beyond `x`, extra forward jumps only push the bug further from home.

## Approach

1. Put `forbidden` in a set `blocked` and compute the right edge `limit`.
2. Keep `seen[0]` (arrived by a right jump, or the start) and `seen[1]` (arrived by a left jump). Start the `queue` with `[0, 0]`.
3. Process one level at a time; `jumps` is the level. If a state stands on `x`, return `jumps`.
4. Jump right to `forward` if it is within `limit`, not blocked and not seen in state 0.
5. Jump left to `backward` only if the last jump was not left, and the spot is non-negative, not blocked and not seen in state 1.
6. If the queue runs dry, `x` is unreachable: return `-1`.

## Example 1, step by step

`forbidden = [14,4,18,1,15]`, `a = 3`, `b = 15`, `x = 9`, so `limit = 18 + 3 + 15 = 36`. Level 0 holds position 0; jumping left would reach -15, so only 3 is added. Level 1 holds 3 and adds 6, level 2 holds 6 and adds 9. At level 3 the state on 9 equals `x`, so the answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + L) where `n` is the length of `forbidden` and `L = max(x, max(forbidden)) + a + b`: building the set is O(n) and each of the 2L states enters the queue at most once.
- Space: O(L) for the two `seen` arrays and the queue.

## Pitfalls

- Marking only positions as visited (without the last-jump state) can lose answers that reach a spot by a left jump first and need a left jump from it later.
- Without a right edge the search never ends when `x` is unreachable.
- Positions to the right of `x` are allowed; capping the search at `x` misses routes like Example 3.
- When `x = 0` the answer is `0` before any jump.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `blocked` | set of forbidden positions |
| `limit` | rightmost position worth exploring |
| `seen` | `seen[s][p]`: state (p, s) was already queued |
| `queue` | states `[position, wentBack]` at the current level |
| `jumps` | number of jumps made to reach the current level |
| `forward`, `backward` | landing spots of a right or left jump |

narration.3: No optimal route needs to go further right than this edge, so the search stays finite.
narration.4: seen[0] marks positions reached by a right jump (or the start), seen[1] those reached by a left jump.
narration.6: The search starts at position 0 with no left jump just made.
narration.9: Each pass of this loop handles every state that needs the same number of jumps.
narration.11: Take each state of the current level: where the bug stands and whether its last jump went left.
narration.12: Breadth-first order means the first time we stand on x uses the fewest jumps.
narration.13: Return the level number as the answer.
narration.16: A right jump is allowed if it stays inside the edge, avoids forbidden spots and is new in state 0.
narration.18: Queue the landing spot, remembering that this jump went right.
narration.21: A left jump needs the last jump to have gone right, a non-negative landing spot that is not forbidden and not yet seen in state 1.
narration.23: Queue the landing spot, remembering that this jump went left.
narration.26: Move on to the states one jump further away.
narration.27: Count the jump that leads to the next level.
narration.29: Every reachable state was explored without landing on x, so home cannot be reached.
